lines: Run it for real, first, without the change: a handful of requests, each one replied to the moment it's handed off, long before any of the real work behind it is even close to done.

Does the client actually feel that difference, the way the guess said it would?
answer: Waiting for real work to finish costs real time, and now that cost shows up exactly where it was expected to.

lines: One real, well-known field guide to exactly this kind of problem says it plainly, in its own words.
First, come up with a real, specific guess about what's actually going on. Then, measure the real system and see whether what you find actually backs that guess up, or knocks it down.
steps.takeaway: Writing the guess down before checking it is what actually lets a real result confirm it or contradict it.

lines: So here's what this topic's own two real runs were really standing in for: a real guess, written down before anything changes, a real change made on purpose, and a real result measured the exact same way both times.
Without that written guess, the exact same slower number would just be a number, with nothing to say whether it was actually expected or not.
With it, that same number either backs up what was predicted, or it doesn't, and either way, that's a real answer instead of a feeling.
